answers.text: Same as before really — give it a template: delivery date, item and quantity, and the change from the order, always in that order. That keeps the three lines the same each time.
List each claim with date, amount, category and submitter, then total up the amounts at the end. Same structure every time so two people would end up with the same numbers.
The dates don't add up — 14th to 19th isn't three days, so something's inconsistent there. Worth checking before it's sent.
62 vs 54 last week is roughly the 15% they say. But 3 late out of 62 isn't a 97% on-time rate, it's closer to 95%, so that figure needs correcting.
I'd go with Output 2 since it gives you the actual sales and returns numbers behind the 4.1%. Output 1 just gives the final figure with nothing behind it.

Reply 2, because it has an order reference and a credit reference to check against. Reply 1 doesn't back up the claim that it won't happen again — though if that could be checked, it could probably go out too.
1. No, that's the customer's own detail. 2. Yes. 3. No, that's not released yet. 4. Better to leave that one too, it's still company material. 5. No.
Wouldn't paste the pricing and discount numbers straight in, and I'd be careful with the confidentiality clause too since it names both sides. Not sure about the rest, would probably ask first.
I'd spot-check some of the figures against the system before sending the report on, so it's not just a read-through.

The order-reading step at the start is the risky one, since a wrong read carries through everything after it. But the real gate should sit right before the confirmation is auto-sent — I'd have it check that the extracted quantity actually matches what's in the warehouse system before anything goes out automatically.
